title: Putting Kid Ory in his band at Billy Berg's Capri
summary: Bigard hired a down-and-out Ory, who had worked for his uncle in New Orleans and was getting $12 a week, with Red Mack and Charlie Mingus, and Ory stole the show with 'Muskrat Ramble' and 'Ory's Creole Trombone'.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: You said when you started -- you headed your own group --
Who did you work with? Who'd you have with you?

Oh, I can't think of those guys. I took Ory. I took him because he used to work with my uncle. He was in New Orleans. He had the band, my uncle, you see, and then a lot of people didn't know this, too. All Dixieland bands, they had to have a fiddle player to lead them, and my uncle was a fiddle player.
Emile, yeah. And Ory had the band and he worked for Ory.

Then when I came here Ory was sweeping the morgue or something, getting about $12 a week. And so I told him, 'C'mon, I'm going to give you a job.' Ory said, 'I can't play music like you're going to play.' I said, 'Don't worry about what
I'm going to play." I said, "C'mon with me."
So I had -- Red Mack was the trumpet. I had Charlie Mingus.

I had -- Those were the two most important ones I had. I had a good drummer. Oh, the drummer, he works with -- oh, God -- Ray Charles, I think. Ray Charles. He's working with Ray Charles. I can't think of his name.

And I asked Ory what could he play and he said he could play "Muskrat Ramble" and "Ory's Creole Trombone". I said, "Yeah." So the guys in the band said, "What do you want that old man in the band for? He can't play nothing." I said, "Well, he's going to play in my band." So I said, "Don't worry about it. We're going to play what we want. But I got a point to make and we're going to play a couple of his tunes. That's all he's going to play."

So we went and rehearsed these two tunes for him. We were opening at Billy Bird's/Borg Capri's that night. The place was packed and jammed and a good group, too. And we got a little hand, you know, and it began to worry me, see. We ain't doing nothing.

Little did I know that there was a lot of Dixieland fans in there, you know. I didn't know it. So I said, "Okay, "Dud" -- I used to called him "Dud" -- I said, "You're ready?" I said, "You're going on now." He's scared; he's trembling.
I said, "What are you trembling about. This is your do or die bit now."

So we played 'Muskrat Ramble' and it broke up the house. And I told the cats in the band, I said, "Look at that. He's stealing all our stuff. He's getting all the applause and we're not getting anything." And I had to turn around, I had to introduce him, tell them who he was, and most of them knew who he was but they hadn't seen him. They didn't know him personally, you know. They had heard of him.
Then when I played 'Ory's Creole Trombone', well, that did it. And he had a good job, from $12 a week I gave him 80-something dollars, about $82.
And he played steadily after that, didn't he?

Yeah, and from then on -- I told him, "Now, get your band together now. Get your band that you brought up here from New Orleans." He brought a band here from New Orleans, you know. I said, "Oh, bring them and rehearse them." I said, "Some people would want to give you a job."
